match.reason: Neither bank point teaches peak or RMS values of an AC supply; the transformer and back emf cards only mention AC in passing, so no bank point covers the idea.

draft.title: Peak and RMS values
card: An AC voltage swings between a positive and a negative peak. The peak voltage, Vpeak, is the largest value it reaches.
The RMS voltage is the DC voltage that would give the same power in a resistor. For a sinusoidal supply, Vrms = Vpeak ÷ √2, which is about 0.71 × Vpeak.
The RMS value is smaller than the peak, because the AC voltage is at its peak only for an instant in each cycle.
The same rule works for current: Irms = Ipeak ÷ √2. Mains voltage is quoted as an RMS value.
draft.remember: RMS is the DC equivalent for power: peak divided by √2.

a.q: An AC supply has a peak voltage of 20 V. About what DC voltage would give the same power in a resistor?
a.why: The equal-power DC voltage is the RMS value: 20 ÷ √2 ≈ 14 V. Multiplying by √2 gives 28 V, which reverses the relationship, as the RMS value is below the peak.

b.q: A workshop in Ballarat has an AC supply with an RMS voltage of 230 V. What is the peak voltage of this supply, to the nearest volt?
b.why: Vpeak = Vrms × √2 = 230 × 1.414 ≈ 325 V. Dividing by √2 gives 163 V, but the quoted 230 V is already the RMS value, so the peak must be larger.
b.clue: The quoted mains value is RMS, and the peak is higher.

check.summary: No problems found. The card, the remember line and both answers check out: 20 ÷ √2 ≈ 14 V, 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V, and Australian mains is quoted as an RMS value.
